questions.q: According to the chapter, for about how long was urban life largely absent in India after the Harappan cities disintegrated?
questions.a: The book says that for a whole millennium urban life remained absent. 'A few centuries' is the delay for iron to become common, a look-alike figure from the same chapter.
o: About a thousand years, a whole millennium
A few centuries, the time iron took to enter daily life
About a hundred years before new towns appeared
About two thousand years, until the British period

questions.q:
A museum in Patna must fill the wall between Panel X, a Harappan city, and Panel Y, a walled city of the Ganga plains in the 1st millennium BCE, with one model. Curator Meera proposes a village of huts and farm tools. Curator Arun proposes a small town somewhere in north India.
(a) What does the chapter say about the length and nature of the gap between the two panels?
(b) Which statement in the chapter would support Arun's small town?
(c) Name three Harappan components that Meera's village model should leave out.
(d) Which model should the museum choose? Decide, weighing both curators against the chapter.
questions.a: (a) About a thousand years; urban life was largely absent. (b) The book says there may have been a few towns here and there in north India. (c) Any three of the Harappan components. (d) Either: the village model fits 'largely absent' and reverting to village life; the small town fits 'a few towns'. The stronger answer picks the village as the typical picture and adds a note that a few towns may have existed.
s: Part (a): about a thousand years, urban life largely absent
Part (b): there may have been a few towns here and there in north India
Part (c): three of writing, sanitation, markets, administration, specialised occupations
Part (d): reasoned choice, ideally with a label hedging 'largely' absent

questions.q: The new phase of urbanisation in the 1st millennium BCE began in which part of the Subcontinent, spreading later to other parts?
questions.a: The book names the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions. Southern cities emerged later, from about 400 BCE.
o: The Ganga plains and parts of the Indus (Sindhu) basin
The southern kingdoms of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas
The central region near the Godavari river only
The Northeast and the western ports

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Second Urbanisation is known only from archaeological excavations.
Reason (R): Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain literatures are full of references to the new urban centres.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the book names two sources, excavations and ancient literature. R is true.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

questions.q: Why is the phase that began in the 1st millennium BCE called the 'Second' Urbanisation? Give two points from the chapter.
questions.a: India's first urban phase was the Harappan civilisation; after it faded, urban life was largely absent for about a thousand years, so the new phase counts as a second one.
s: The first phase was the Harappan civilisation
A gap of about a thousand years with little urban life lay between the two

questions.q: At a site in the Indus basin, archaeologists find a thin layer of mud huts, grinding stones and clay pots from about 1500 BCE, with no drains, no seals and no big buildings. How should the layer be read?
questions.a: The layer lacks writing, sanitation, markets and public structures, so it shows people who reverted to village life. A janapada capital would be a clan territory's centre; the Indus basin is only one region where the later phase began, and the layer is far too early for it; mahajanapada capitals were fortified.
o: As the village life of the millennium after Harappa, when urban components had gone
As a janapada capital, since janapadas were led by a raja
As a site of the Second Urbanisation, since it lies in the Indus basin
As a mahajanapada capital whose moat has been filled up over time

questions.q: A student reads a Jain text describing a busy walled city in the Ganga plains and writes in her notebook that the city definitely existed. Which step would a historian add before accepting this?
questions.a: The book names archaeological excavations as what confirmed the existence of the centres. Trusting the text alone relies on one source type; looking for Harappan sanitation mixes in the Harappan phase; checking the list of 16 brings in another topic.
o: Look for excavated remains, since excavations have confirmed such centres
Trust the text alone, because ancient literature is full of references to such cities
Look for a Harappan-style sanitation system at the site, since all cities had one
Check the usual list of 16 mahajanapadas to see if the city is named there

questions.q: A classmate's timeline entry reads: 'c. 1900 BCE - Harappan cities fade. The very next century - cities rise in the Ganga plains.' Using the chapter's time frame, show that this entry cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says urban life remained absent for a whole millennium, about ten times longer than one century, so the Ganga-plains cities rose about a thousand years later.
s: States the gap the book gives: a whole millennium without urban life
Compares: next century is only 100 years against about 1000
Concludes the cities of the Ganga plains belong to the 1st millennium BCE, long after the break

questions.q: Rohan says: 'After the Harappan cities were abandoned, there was no town anywhere in India until the Second Urbanisation began.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Not fully. The book says urban life was largely absent but there may have been a few towns here and there in north India, and important regional cultures existed.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the absolute claim
Reason: urban life was largely, not totally, absent for about a thousand years
Evidence: a few towns may have existed in north India and regional cultures continued

questions.q:
The history teacher of a Pune school shows a chart of a site called Kheda. Layer 1: a planned town, abandoned around 1900 BCE. Layers 2 to 4: only huts and farm tools, with people living there without a break until about 900 BCE. Layer 5: a gateway with a water-filled ditch outside it, and an ancient text that names the place. The students must write a caption for the whole chart.
(a) Work out the break in town life shown by the chart, say which phase Layer 5 belongs to, and say whether the break fits the book's figure.
(b) Name three components of the Harappan urban order that Layers 2 to 4 lack.
(c) The text in Layer 5 names the place. Why should a historian not rely on the text alone, and what do the layers add?
(d) Choose a caption: 'Kheda: the city that vanished' or 'Kheda: a place where life never stopped'. Judge both against the chapter's 'largely absent, but a few towns may have existed'.
questions.a: (a) 1900 - 900 = 1000 years; Layer 5 is the Second Urbanisation; it matches the whole millennium. (b) Any three of the components in the book's list. (c) The book says excavations confirmed the centres that literature mentions; the layers give physical evidence. (d) Either can be defended: 'vanished' fits urban life being largely absent, 'never stopped' fits people living there and the possibility of a few towns; the best answer qualifies the caption, since life continued but as a village.
s: Part (a): 1000 years; Second Urbanisation; matches the whole millennium
Part (b): three of writing, sanitation, markets, administration, specialised occupations, public buildings
Part (c): excavations confirm the existence of centres that texts only describe
Part (d): weighs both captions; best answer qualifies either

questions.q: (a) Name the two kinds of evidence by which we know of the Second Urbanisation. (b) Why does a historian gain more from using both than from using only one?
questions.a: (a) Archaeological excavations and ancient literature. (b) Texts describe the urban centres and digs confirm that they really existed, so each covers what the other cannot.
s: Part (a): archaeological excavations and ancient literature
Part (b): literature describes the centres and excavations confirm they existed

questions.q:
Match the item in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. First Urbanisation  2. Second Urbanisation  3. Archaeological excavations  4. Ancient literature
Column II: a. Confirmed that the ancient urban centres existed  b. The Indus/Harappan/Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation  c. Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts mentioning new centres  d. Began in the Ganga plains in the 1st millennium BCE and continues today
questions.a: First-Harappan, Second-1st millennium BCE onward, excavations-confirmed, literature-texts. Pairs 3 and 4 are the easy ones to swap.

questions.q: Which pair of sources does the chapter give for knowing that the Second Urbanisation happened?
questions.a: The book says: mainly (1) archaeological excavations and (2) ancient literature (late Vedic, Buddhist, Jain). Coins and inscriptions appear elsewhere in the chapter but are not the two named sources.
o: Archaeological excavations and ancient literature
Punch-marked coins and inscriptions on temple walls
Harappan seals and the timeline of the chapter
Maps of the sixteen mahajanapadas and Kautilya's quotation

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The Second Urbanisation was confined to the Ganga plains and never reached other regions.
Statement 2: Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain literatures are full of references to the new urban centres.
Statement 3: In some Harappan cities, people continued living after the urban order ended, but with a rural or village lifestyle.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the new phase gradually spread to other parts of the Subcontinent. 2 and 3 are as the book says.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Compare the First and the Second Urbanisation in India on four points: the metal in use, one effect of the new metal, what happened to each afterwards, and where the second began.
questions.a: First: Harappan, copper and bronze, disintegrated early in the 2nd millennium BCE. Second: 1st millennium BCE, iron (which helped agriculture on a bigger scale), began in the Ganga plains and parts of the Indus basin, spread, and continues today.
s: Metals: copper and bronze for the First, iron for the Second
One effect of iron: agriculture on a bigger scale or lighter, sharper weapons
Fate of the First: it disintegrated and urban life was largely absent
Fate of the Second: it spread and continues to today
Region: the Ganga plains and parts of the Indus basin

questions.q: Write three short sentences as a letter from a potter whose Harappan city is being abandoned, telling a cousin in a village what the city is losing. Use three different components of the Harappan urban order.
questions.a: Any three from: elaborate public and private structures, crowded streets and busy markets, specialised communities of metalsmiths, potters, builders, weavers, a writing system, a sanitation system, an administration and a ruling class.
s: Names a first component such as busy markets or crowded streets
Names a second component such as writing or sanitation
Names a third component such as administration or specialised craft communities

questions.q: (a) From the list - writing system, iron tools, sanitation system, punch-marked coins - pick the two that belonged to the Harappan urban order. (b) Name one of the other two and say which phase of urban life it belongs with.
questions.a: (a) Writing system and sanitation system. (b) Iron tools (iron metallurgy) or coins belong with the Second Urbanisation; the Harappans mastered copper and bronze.
s: Part (a): writing system and sanitation system
Part (b): iron tools or coins, with the Second Urbanisation

questions.q: (a) Name any two components of the Harappan urban order that had disappeared. (b) What did people who stayed on in some of those cities go back to, and why was city life no longer possible for them?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: elaborate structures, busy markets, specialised communities, writing, sanitation, administration, a state with a ruling class. (b) A rural or village lifestyle; the components that made city life possible were gone.
s: Part (a): two components such as writing system, sanitation, markets, administration
Part (b): a rural or village lifestyle because the urban components had disappeared

questions.q: What is meant by the 'Second Urbanisation' of India? Name the region where it began.
questions.a: A new phase of city life that began in the 1st millennium BCE and, incidentally, has continued right up to today. It began in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions.
s: Meaning: a new phase of urban life in the 1st millennium BCE, continuing to today
Region: the Ganga plains (and parts of the Indus basin)

questions.q: Explain, with at least four components of the Harappan urban order, why a place that lost them could no longer be called a city. Then name the two kinds of evidence by which we know the later urban phase and the three literatures that describe it.
questions.a: Structures, busy markets, specialised occupations, writing, sanitation, administration and a ruling state had disappeared, so people went back to village life. The Second Urbanisation is known from archaeological excavations and ancient literature: late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain.
s: Names at least four components of the urban order
Explains that without them a settlement reverted to a rural or village life
Names the two kinds of evidence: excavations and ancient literature
Names late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain literatures

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT among the components of the Harappan urban order that had disappeared by the early 2nd millennium BCE?
questions.a: The book lists structures, markets, specialised occupations, writing, sanitation, administration and a state structure. Iron is the technology of the Second Urbanisation; the Harappans mastered copper and bronze.
o: Widespread use of iron tools
A writing system
A sanitation system
Communities with specialised occupations such as metalsmiths and potters

questions.q: What is a moat? State its purpose in a mahajanapada capital.
questions.a: A moat is a deep, wide ditch filled with water surrounding a fort or a fortified city; capitals had one outside the fortifications as further defence.
s: Meaning: a deep, wide ditch around a fort or fortified city, filled with water
Purpose: further defence outside the fortifications

questions.q:
The municipal council of Rajgir in Bihar plans to rebuild one feature of the old capital for visitors. The old city had a thick rampart, a wide water-filled ditch outside it, and a gateway through the wall that was only a few metres wide. The council can afford only one feature.
(a) What is the water-filled ditch called, and of which mahajanapada was Rajagriha (Rajgir) the capital?
(b) State the purpose of the ditch and the purpose of the narrow gateway.
(c) What does the chapter say about most ancient capitals of the mahajanapadas today?
(d) Which feature should the council rebuild to show best how the state ruled? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) A moat; Magadha. (b) The moat gave further defence; the narrow gateway let guards control the movement of people and goods. (c) Most are living cities, often 2,500 years old. (d) Either: the narrow gateway, since it shows control of people and goods; or the moat, since it shows defence of the capital. Marks for a chapter-based reason.
s: Part (a): a moat; Magadha
Part (b): moat for defence; narrow gateway so guards could control people and goods
Part (c): most continue to be living cities, often 2,500 years old
Part (d): a reasoned choice, defence or control

questions.q: By roughly when had some early janapadas merged to form bigger units known as mahajanapadas?
questions.a: The book gives the 8th or 7th centuries BCE. The other dates belong to the Harappan break, the southern cities and the end of the mahajanapadas.
o: By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE
By the early 2nd millennium BCE, soon after the Harappan cities faded
By about 400 BCE, when southern cities began to emerge
By 300 or 200 BCE, when the mahajanapadas ceased to exist

questions.q: Name the four most powerful of the new states, and give the capital of any one of them.
questions.a: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti. Capitals: Magadha - Rajagriha, Kosala - Shravasti, Vatsa - Kaushambi, Avanti - Ujjayini.
s: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti
One correct capital such as Rajagriha for Magadha or Kaushambi for Vatsa

questions.q:
Match the mahajanapada in Column I with its capital in Column II.
Column I: 1. Magadha  2. Kosala  3. Vatsa  4. Avanti
Column II: a. Ujjayini  b. Kaushambi  c. Rajagriha  d. Shravasti
questions.a: Magadha-Rajagriha, Kosala-Shravasti, Vatsa-Kaushambi, Avanti-Ujjayini.

questions.q: Set a two-mark question of your own whose answer is 'Ashmaka', and write its model answer. The question must give two different clues about the state.
questions.a: Example: Name the state of the usual list of 16 that lay in central India, close to the Godavari River. Answer: Ashmaka.
s: Question gives a clue about where the state lay, e.g. near the Godavari
Question gives a second, different clue, e.g. central India or the usual list of 16
Model answer names Ashmaka and agrees with both clues

questions.q: A student says: 'The mahajanapadas came first; the clans settled into janapadas only after the large states had formed.' Use the chapter's dates to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The book says clans became associated with janapadas towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, and that by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some of these merged into mahajanapadas, so the order is janapada then mahajanapada.
s: Janapadas were clan territories towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE
Mahajanapadas formed by merging, by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE
So janapadas came first and mahajanapadas later

questions.q: Describe how janapadas grew into mahajanapadas, naming the factors that helped, and explain why the chapter does not give a single fixed list of them.
questions.a: Clans with common language and customs became associated with territories led by a raja (janapadas), which grew as trade networks connected them. By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some merged into mahajanapadas. The texts have different lists, the more frequent has 16, and a few more or smaller janapadas may have existed.
s: Clans linked to a territory under a raja formed janapadas
Trade networks expanded and connected the janapadas
Some merged by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE into mahajanapadas
The more frequent list names 16, from Gandhara to Anga to Ashmaka
The texts give different lists; a few more and smaller janapadas may have existed

questions.q: Which set of reasons does the chapter offer for so many mahajanapadas lying in the Ganga plains?
questions.a: These are the 'Think About It' reasons. The defences option lists features of capitals; the Sanchi and Kodumanal option mixes up later examples; the routes option wrongly starts both routes in the plains.
o: Fertile farmland, iron ore in nearby hills, and new trade networks
Moats, ramparts and narrow gateways that made the plains easy to defend
Silver for coins, a smithy at Sanchi and shell industries at Kodumanal
The Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, which both began in the plains

questions.q:
Ananya's group in a Kolkata school makes a chart of the 16 mahajanapadas of the usual list. Their own count puts 10 of the 16 inside the Ganga plains and the other six outside. The group has time to study only one reason in depth for the clustering inside the plains.
(a) Name the state at the northwestern end of the usual list and the one in central India near the Godavari; both lie outside the plains.
(b) What percentage of the 16 does the group's count put inside the plains?
(c) Name two reasons the book suggests for the clustering in the plains.
(d) Which one reason should the group study to understand states like those in part (a) as well? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Gandhara and Ashmaka. (b) 62.5 percent. (c) Any two of: agriculture on fertile land, iron ore in mountains and hills, new trade networks. (d) Trade networks, since the book says janapadas grew as trade networks connected them; iron ore in hills is also defensible if justified.
s: Part (a): Gandhara and Ashmaka
Part (b): 10/16 = 62.5 percent
Part (c): two of fertile agriculture, iron ore, new trade networks
Part (d): a reasoned choice, such as trade networks that connected janapadas

questions.q: A guide describes a state of the usual list that lay in central India, close to the Godavari River. Which state is she describing?
questions.a: The book places Ashmaka in central India near the Godavari. Gandhara is the northwestern end, Anga the eastern end, and Magadha is in part of today's Bihar.
o: Ashmaka
Gandhara
Anga
Magadha

questions.q: In an ancient region, a clan settled in a territory led by a raja. Centuries later that territory and others merged into one larger state. Which pair of terms, in this order, names the two stages?
questions.a: Janapada then mahajanapada is the right order. Reversing it is wrong; the pairs that start with a gana mix the republic type into the question about territory and size.
o: Janapada, then mahajanapada
Mahajanapada, then janapada
Gana, then janapada
Mahajanapada, then gana

questions.q: State two features of the capitals of the mahajanapadas.
questions.a: Any two of: fairly large well-fortified cities; a moat outside the fortification; deliberately narrow gateways so guards could control people and goods; most continue to be living cities today.
s: First feature, such as fortified, large city, moat
Second feature, such as narrow gateways for control or still a living city today

questions.q: (a) Name the mahajanapada at the northwestern end and the one at the eastern end of the usual list of 16. (b) Ashmaka lay close to which river, and why does its position show that the mahajanapadas were not all in the Ganga plains?
questions.a: (a) Gandhara in the northwest and Anga in the east. (b) The Godavari River; Ashmaka was in central India, far from the Ganga plains.
s: Part (a): Gandhara and Anga
Part (b): Godavari, central India, so outside the Ganga plains

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The usual list of mahajanapadas names 16 states, though the texts give different lists.
Statement 2: Most mahajanapada capitals were fairly large, well-fortified cities with a moat outside the fortifications.
Statement 3: All sixteen mahajanapadas of the usual list lay inside the Ganga plains.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: the list runs from Gandhara in the northwest to Anga in the east and to Ashmaka in central India, so only many, not all, lay in the Ganga plains.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: 'The Ganga plains were the heartland of the mahajanapadas.' Justify the statement.
questions.a: Many of the 16 mahajanapadas were concentrated in the Ganga plains: fertile agriculture, iron ore in mountains and hills, and new trade networks. But not all lay there: Gandhara in the northwest and Ashmaka in central India.
s: States that many of the 16 were concentrated in the Ganga plains
Reason: growth of agriculture on fertile land
Reason: iron ore in the mountains and hills
Reason: formation of new trade networks
Qualifies with an outlying example such as Gandhara or Ashmaka

questions.q: The Sanskrit word 'janapada' means, in the book's words,
questions.a: The correct meaning is where the people have set foot. The council meaning is the sabha or samiti; the merged large state is a mahajanapada; the fortified city is a capital.
o: where the people (jana) have set foot (pada)
the council where matters concerning the clan were discussed
a large state formed when several early states merged
a fortified capital with a moat and narrow gateways

questions.q: (a) What helped the janapadas grow, according to the chapter? (b) How did this lead to the larger units called mahajanapadas?
questions.a: (a) The janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them. (b) Connected janapadas merged by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, and the bigger units were called mahajanapadas.
s: Part (a): trade networks expanded and connected them
Part (b): some janapadas merged by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE into mahajanapadas

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many ancient capitals of the mahajanapadas continue to be living cities today.
Reason (R): The mahajanapadas ceased to exist by about 300 or 200 BCE.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the end of the mahajanapadas does not explain why their capitals are still cities.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT among the four most powerful of the new states named in the chapter?
questions.a: The book names Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti as most powerful. Gandhara is on the list of 16 but is only mentioned as the northwestern end.
o: Gandhara
Magadha
Vatsa
Avanti

questions.q: A museum caption reads: 'There were exactly 16 mahajanapadas, and every capital was a small unfortified village.' Find the two errors and correct each using the chapter.
questions.a: Error 1: the more frequent list names 16, but texts differ and a few more or smaller janapadas may have existed. Error 2: most capitals were large well-fortified cities with a moat. Corrected: 'The usual list names 16 mahajanapadas, most with large fortified capitals.'
s: First error: 'exactly 16' - the texts give different lists, 16 is the more frequent
Second error: capitals were fairly large well-fortified cities with a moat
Gives a corrected caption

questions.q: Why do scholars call Vajji and Malla 'early republics'?
questions.a: They are called early republics because the assembly decided and selected the ruler. 'No assembly or ruler' is false; inherited rule describes monarchies; being largest is not claimed by the book.
o: Assembly decided by vote and chose the ruler
They had no assembly and no ruler of any kind
Their rajas inherited the throne from their fathers
They were the largest and most powerful states of the time

questions.q: In a state, a council debated whether to raise a new army. Members voted when they disagreed, and the same council then chose who should be ruler. How would the book describe this state?
questions.a: Monarchies had hereditary rulers, and the council that voted and chose the ruler marks a gana. The 'janapada with only small states having assemblies' idea is wrong since every janapada had an assembly.
o: A gana or sangha, an early republic
A monarchy like Magadha, since every state had a raja
A janapada, since only smaller states had assemblies
A mahajanapada with no assembly at all

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT a duty the chapter expects of the raja of a monarchy?
questions.a: The duties named are taxes, law and order, fortifications and an army. Preserving knowledge and performing rituals is the varna role of Brahmins, not a duty of the raja.
o: Preserving knowledge and performing rituals
Maintaining law and order across the territory
Building fortifications around his own capital
Maintaining an army to defend the territory

questions.q:
A student's project on janapadas says: 'In ancient India an assembly could remove any ruler.' Her teacher asks her to check every word of the sentence against the chapter before the project is displayed.
(a) What was the council of each janapada called, and who were most of its members?
(b) What was a good ruler supposed to do about the advice of assemblies?
(c) What do some texts say about an incompetent ruler, and what caution does the book add?
(d) Rewrite the project's sentence so that it stays true to the chapter, and name the words you changed.
questions.a: (a) Sabha or samiti; mostly elders. (b) Take their advice, with ministers and administrators, and not rule arbitrarily. (c) Some texts say an incompetent ruler could be removed by the assembly, but this was not an established law since the data for such remote periods is incomplete. (d) 'According to some texts, an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler.' Changed: added 'according to some texts', replaced 'any' by 'an incompetent'.
s: Part (a): sabha or samiti; mostly elders of the clan
Part (b): take advice from assemblies, ministers and administrators
Part (c): some texts say he could be removed; not an established law, data incomplete
Part (d): rewrite hedges with 'according to some texts' and 'incompetent', replacing 'any'

questions.q:
Match the state in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Magadha  2. Kosala  3. Avanti  4. Vajji
Column II: a. Located in part of today's Bihar  b. Located in part of today's Uttar Pradesh  c. Located in part of today's Madhya Pradesh  d. A gana whose assembly could select the ruler
questions.a: Magadha - Bihar, Kosala - Uttar Pradesh, Avanti - Madhya Pradesh; Vajji - gana. Kosala and Avanti are the pair most easily swapped.

questions.q: (a) Name the body in each janapada where matters concerning the clan were discussed. (b) How did its power in a gana differ from its power in a monarchy?
questions.a: (a) The sabha or samiti. (b) In a monarchy the raja was the ultimate authority, supported by ministers and the assembly; in a gana the assembly took important decisions by discussion and vote and even selected the ruler.
s: Part (a): sabha or samiti
Part (b): advisory in a monarchy, deciding and choosing the ruler in a gana

questions.q:
At a Class 7 civics fair, two groups present models of governance. Group Green: decisions are taken by discussion in a sabha and by vote when members disagree, and the same body picks the head. Group Blue: the head follows the family line, and listens to a council of elders before deciding himself. The jury will give one prize for the model that best shows the idea that a ruler 'was not expected to rule arbitrarily'.
(a) Which group matches Vajji and which matches Magadha?
(b) Name one other mahajanapada that fits each group.
(c) Why do scholars call Green's type of state 'early republics'?
(d) Which group should get the prize? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Green is Vajji; Blue is Magadha. (b) Malla; Kosala or Avanti. (c) Because the assembly decided and selected the ruler. (d) Either: Blue, since the book says a good ruler took advice from assemblies, ministers and administrators; or Green, since there the assembly itself decided and chose the ruler. Marks for a chapter-based reason.
s: Part (a): Green - Vajji; Blue - Magadha
Part (b): Malla for Green; Kosala or Avanti for Blue
Part (c): the assembly selected the ruler and took major decisions by discussion and vote
Part (d): a reasoned choice

questions.q: Show that one mahajanapada cannot be both a hereditary monarchy with the raja as ultimate authority and a gana in which the assembly selects the ruler.

Three students plan projects for an exhibition called 'Connected India'. Karan will show the road that begins at Kaushambi. questions.a: (a) Dakshinapatha, Vindhya Range; Sisupalgarh, Kalinga; Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas. (b) Karan: a route linking the Ganga plains to the south; Leela: a planned, fortified city beyond the plains; Mohan: southern cities and kingdoms trading in India and overseas. (c) Mohan's. Part (c): Mohan's, since the south traded with kingdoms overseas
Part (d): a reasoned choice weighing the three
